Dear Chairpersons Skinner, Ting, Portantino, Holden, and Ms. Bosler:
Pursuant to Assembly Bill 128 (Chapter 21, Statutes of 2021), this report and supporting
documents outline the total costs of the September 14, 2021, Gubernatorial Recall
Election.
Background
On June 23, 2021, the Secretary of State notified the Department of Finance that a
sufficient number of verified signatures had been submitted to initiate a recall election
against the Governor.
On July 1, 2021, the Department of Finance notified the Governor, the Secretary of
State and the Chairpersons of the Joint Legislative Budget Committee of the estimated
costs of the gubernatorial recall election (See Department of Finance letter (ca.gov))
Assembly Bill 128 (Chapter 21, Statutes of 2021) was passed by the Legislature and
signed by the Governor, which provides that:
(a) For the conduct of the election concerning the recall of the Governor during
the 2021-22 fiscal year, $215,234,000 is appropriated from the General Fund.
The Legislature determines this amount is reasonably necessary to conduct the
recall election and designates these funds for that purpose.
(b) Notwithstanding any other law, the Controller shall allocate these funds to
counties according to a schedule provided by the Department of Finance. Any
excess funds received by the county shall be used to offset state costs for the
next election conducted by the county. Each county shall report its final total cost
to administer the gubernatorial recall election to the Secretary of State in a
manner and by a date determined by the Secretary of State.
(c) No later than February 1, 2022, the Secretary of State shall report on the final
costs of the gubernatorial recall election to the Department of Finance and the
Joint Legislative Budget Committee. It is the intent of the Legislature to consider
making adjustments to this appropriation based on that report.
The report shall include the following:
(1) The total cost of the gubernatorial recall election by county.
(2) The costs broken out by category for each county.
(3) Any funds remaining, by county, that can be used to offset state costs for the
next election conducted by the county.
Subsequently, Senate Bill 152 (Chapter 34, Statutes of 2021) made changes to how the
2021 gubernatorial recall election was to be held, including requiring it to be held as a
regular election. As a result, the Department of Finance requested updated cost
estimates from counties to administer the recall election under the provisions of Senate
Bill 152. The updated estimated costs provided by counties was $243,583,308.50.
Additionally, Senate Bill 152 provides:
The sum of thirty-five million dollars ($35,000,000) is hereby appropriated from
the General Fund to the Secretary of State for the purpose of supporting
statewide and county costs related to administering the 2021 gubernatorial recall
election. It is the intent of the Legislature to consider adjustments to this amount
based on the final costs of the gubernatorial recall election.
On July 20, 2021, the Department of Finance requested that the State Controller’s
Office remit payment to county elections officials for the 2021 California gubernatorial
recall election in a sum totaling $243,583,308. (See Allocation and Recall Election
Costs Letter)
Subsequently, California’s 58 counties received payment from the State Controller’s
Office as requested by the Department of Finance and successfully conducted the
September 14, 2021, Gubernatorial Recall Election.

As a result of Assembly Bill 128 and Senate Bill 152, $243,583,308.50 was allocated to

cost of the gubernatorial recall election was $200,241,680, which includes

Key Findings
The California election has entered its final stretch, with the governor’s race at the top of the ticket and 52 House races that will help determine the party in control of the 120th Congress. The November 3 ballot also includes 14 state propositions—five legislative measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—the most since the November 2016 election. The 2025–26 legislative session ended in late August with a flurry of bills sent to Governor Newsom to sign or veto in September. The recent trends in job growth, consumer prices, and interest rates send mixed signals about the US and California economy.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey on topics including the November races, legislative ballot measures, and citizens’ initiatives, as well as state and national issues that was conducted September 4–September 10, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) continues to lead Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a similarly wide margin (62% to 36%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty-five percent say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote. Fifty-eight percent say that voting is more important this year than in past midterms. After reading the ballot titles and labels, majorities would vote yes on Proposition 1 (55%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (60%; Rainy Day Fund). Three other legislative ballot measures fall short of a majority.
Fifty-two percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would also vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (61%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (55%; Immunology Bond), Proposition 41 (51%; Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), and Proposition 42 (54%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Partisans vary in their support for these citizens’ initiatives. Three other citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Overwhelming majorities agree that there are too many propositions on the state ballot.
Majorities of adults and likely voters think that the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Fifty-one percent of adults and likely voters say that they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance, while 45 percent of adults and 48 percent of likely voters approve of the state legislature. Majorities of adults and likely voters report that recent price increases have caused financial hardships for their household. Seventy percent of Californians think that the state is divided into economic groups, the haves and have-nots. Majorities of adults and likely voters say that they can trust the state government in Sacramento to do what is right “only some of the time.”
Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-three percent of adults and 27 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while 17 percent of adults and 16 percent of likely voters approve of the US Congress. Seven in ten Californians are dissatisfied with the availability of affordable health care and believe that the US government is responsible for ensuring that all Americans have access to health care. Fewer than half say the major parties have a lot or some good ideas. Overwhelming majorities say they can trust the federal government to do what is right “only some of the time.”
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
The top two vote-getters in the California June primary for statewide elected offices and for federal and state legislative seats are on the November ballot. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom, who is termed out of office. There are 52 House races in California that will help determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will also decide on 14 state propositions this fall—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax measures and multibillion-dollar state bonds.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a wide margin (60% to 38%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. In our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), Becerra led Hilton by 25 points (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 93 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 92 percent of Republicans favor Hilton, while independents lean toward the Democratic candidate (57% Becerra, 38% Hilton). Majorities favor Becerra over Hilton across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and in the state’s major regions except for the Central Valley (46% Becerra, 52% Hilton).
Affordability and the cost of living have been the top issue on Californians’ minds in our recent polling. Sixty-five percent of likely voters say that the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote (30% somewhat, 5% not too important). In our February survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/), the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability were very important to 61 percent of likely voters and to majorities across parties, regions, and demographic groups. Today, majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions hold this view. Notably, partisans are largely in agreement: 69 percent of Democrats, 65 percent of Republicans, and 59 percent of independents say that the gubernatorial candidates’ affordability positions are very important. Becerra supporters (66%) express this opinion as often as Hilton supporters (65%). Seven in ten or more of those who live in the Inland Empire (79%) or Los Angeles (70%), those who have incomes of $40,000 to $99,999 (74%), those who have children 18 or younger in their household (74%), Latinos (71%), renters (70%), and women (70%) say the gubernatorial candidates’ positions on affordability are very important in determining their vote.
Many Californians are watching news about the gubernatorial candidates. About six in ten likely voters say they are following news about candidates for the governor’s election either very (18%) or fairly (40%) closely. By comparison, in our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten likely voters were very (23%) or fairly closely (48%) following the news about candidates in the governor’s election, including majorities across partisan groups (68% Democrats, 76% Republicans, 65% independents) and demographic groups and regions. Similar shares were closely following the news about candidates in the gubernatorial election in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (21% very, 41% fairly), while fewer were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (17% very, 33% fairly), and overwhelming majorities were in September 2021 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2021/) (40% very, 41% fairly) prior to the special election on the recall of Governor Newsom. Today, partisans vary in following the news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely (57% Democrats, 68% Republicans, 50% independents), as do Becerra and Hilton supporters (53% to 69%).
House Races. When asked about their House district race, most likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a wide margin (62% to 36%). Likely voter preferences were similar in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican) and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, likely voters’ preferences for the Democratic candidate and the Republican candidate are similar in the governor’s race and the House race. More than nine in ten Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while independents say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (59% to 36%). Majorities say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district races across demographic groups and major state regions with the exception of the Central Valley (47%).
Many Californians believe that their vote matters in the 2026 midterm election. When asked about the importance of voting this year compared to past midterm elections, 58 percent of likely voters say it is more important, 39 percent say it is about as important as in past years, and only 2 percent say voting is less important to them. Californians are more likely to say that voting in the midterm is more important to them this year than they were in September 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2022/) (43%) and in September 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2018/) (52%). Today, Democratic likely voters (69%) are much more likely than Republicans (50%) and independents (45%) to say that voting in this midterm is more important this year. Majorities across the state’s regions say that voting in this midterm election is more important this year. Those who say they would vote for Democratic candidates (64%) are more likely than those supporting Republican candidates (49%) in their local House races to say that voting is more important to them this year than in past midterms.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We also gauged support for five state propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Fifty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute that authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 43 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (75% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 56% independents) and between homeowners and renters (49% to 72%). Half or more across the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the state’s rainy day fund, approved by voters in 2014 to provide funding for economic downturns; 39 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (82% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 60% independents). Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 2 across age, education, gender, homeownership, and income groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-two percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute that repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 53 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (55% Democrats, 19% Republicans, 41% independents). Half or more would vote no across the state’s major regions.
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Thirty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment; 59 percent would vote no. Support for Proposition 5 falls short of a majority across partisan groups (40% Democrats, 34% Republicans, 28% independents) and across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-three percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment that increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 51 percent would vote no. Support varies across partisan groups (33% Democrats, 61% Republicans, 43% independents) and state regions (60% Central Valley; 50% Orange/San Diego; 43% Los Angeles; 35% Inland Empire; 32% San Francisco Bay Area).
When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 9 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (5% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 1% Proposition 4; 1% Proposition 5; 1% Proposition 43). When California Governor Gray Davis was the subject of a recall effort in 2003, he said in a televised speech (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.htmlhttps:/www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-20-me-davis20-story.html) at UCLA that he thought the recall would damage “the very fabric of our democracy.”
Elected officials may not like to see accountability arrive earlier than expected, but that doesn’t make Californians’ recall powers a threat to democracy.
While Proposition 5 doesn’t attack the people’s ability to hold a recall election, it does tinker with how a replacement candidate is selected.
Related Articles
Endorsement: Break the 49ers' grip over Santa Clara. Elect these three candidates. (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/31/endorsement-break-the-49ers-grip-over-santa-clara-make-kertes-mayor-elect-inciarte-and-crutchlow-to-council/)
Endorsement: These three City Council candidates are San Jose's best choices (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-peter-ortiz-bien-doan-and-genny-altwer-to-san-jose-city-council/)
Endorsement: Elect Michael Melillo to San Jose Unified School District Board of Education (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-michael-melillo-to-san-jose-unified-school-district-board-of-education/)
Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
We urge voters to reject it.
Proposition 5 would eliminate the election of a replacement candidate on the same ballot as a recall. Currently a recall ballot has two questions: 1) Should the elected official be removed, and 2) Choose a candidate to replace that official if the recall is successful.
The measure would remove question 2, eliminating the simultaneous election for a replacement. Instead, if a state official other than a governor was recalled, the office would become vacant and would be filled by special election or appointment, according to existing law. If a governor was recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over and serve until the end of the term or until a special election could be held, depending on timing.
Under current law, a recalled official is barred from running as a replacement candidate in the special election to fill the seat. Proposition 5 changes that as well. In a special election to replace a recalled official, the recalled official could be on the ballot.
These changes turn a process to remove officials from power into a cynical blueprint to keep power in the hands of the same officials. It makes a mockery of the recall, which was designed to empower voters to remove and immediately replace an officeholder for any reason, whether the officeholder thinks the reason is sufficient or not.
Rejecting Proposition 5 is also about preserving the state’s ability to empower unique and independent political voices.
Under current rules, officials who are recalled are succeeded by the candidate seeking that official’s job who gets the most votes at the same time as the recall. This process is why Arnold Schwarzenegger was able to quickly replace the deeply unpopular Davis.
Nearly one million more Californians voted to recall Davis than to retain him, and the Republican Schwarzenegger won a plurality of the replacement vote after running as a pro-business social liberal who wanted the state to lead the global response (https://www.kqed.org/science/1931206/californias-a-team-on-climate-moonbeam-and-the-governator) to climate change.
But if Proposition 5 had been in place, Davis would have been succeeded by Lt. Gov. Cruz Bustamante. He was an uninspiring but mostly baggage-free politician who would have likely been the favorite in a subsequent regular or special election in California to finish Davis’ term, even against Schwarzenegger.
Changing the California Constitution in a way that creates even bigger obstacles to electing independent-minded candidates — while stripping the people of their primary tool of accountability — is a bad idea.
Reject Proposition 5.

In a polarized state where one party has a supermajority, the recall process mainly serves as a tactic by a minority party trying to gain power. This method can remove an official and choose a leader from a different party through a direct-democracy approach, bypassing the usual election cycle. While it can seem like "gaming," it actually requires a majority of current voters to support the removal, making it a legitimate electoral action based on minority plural support, rather than a mere shortcut.**Evaluating legislative support and costs**

Both sides oppose the measure, possibly due to low public awareness. The measure passed by supermajorities but not unanimously. Legislative votes, like the 32-8 in the Senate, suggest almost all Democrats supported it, while some Republicans and maybe Democrats voted no. The official cost analysis is unclear, but with a state budget of around $300 billion, the fiscal impact seems minimal. The recall process also incurs millions, making claims about reducing expenses appear weak.**Analyzing recall propositions**

This measure isn’t about reducing waste; it's about who gets to be in office. The recall aims to remove officials, not to create special elections that reward the best candidate in a crowded field. The current system mismatches majoritarian ideals since a majority can remove someone, but the replacement is selected by a plurality. This invites partisan misuse and can derail normal elections. Prop 5 keeps the recall option for voters, with reasonable succession rules from established processes.**Evaluating the recall process**

When an official is recalled, they can run again in a subsequent special election, allowing voters to choose in a more traditional format, but maybe that's a bit too lenient. The officeholder is immediately removed, so they're not protected. While appointing statewide officials for midterm vacancies gives the governor authority (with legislative confirmation), it temporarily limits voter choice. Crowded replacement ballots can confuse voters, leading to many blanks. A simple yes/no option may improve clarity. Although Prop 5 has its flaws, it appears to enhance the current system overall.**Analyzing electoral propositions**

I’m considering the proposition regarding future elections, but it has some significant flaws. For one, not all successor votes create pluralities after special elections. Another issue is that allowing someone to run again could be problematic — if voters recall someone but they win again in a subsequent election, it means their earlier decision might be reversed. This makes the recall process less straightforward.**Evaluating recall votes**

The recall vote is a straightforward yes or no question, allowing voters to change their minds. In cases of direct democracy, the ability to recall can lead to an election. For governors, if a recall occurs early enough, voters elect a new governor by majority, even if the current one runs again. Regarding Lieutenant Governors, they might serve the remainder of the term following a midterm recall, and the voters' desire for change isn’t always guaranteed; misconduct can be the reason for a recall.**Assessing the recall process**

While a recall might seem more democratic, it can actually complicate voter choice since the direct election of officials is somewhat reduced. In the current system, recall ballots include a replacement vote even if the recall fails, which can confuse voters. This setup diverts attention from the essential question of whether an official should be recalled. Separating these issues could help voters focus better. Additionally, a 2021 poll indicated nearly 70% thought recalls were a waste, particularly when the replacements fail.**Evaluating recall elections**

It seems like the stated fiscal benefits for VIG might be weak, and costs and savings are unclear. However, the measure is about more than just cost; it focuses on majority rule. Recall elections typically have lower turnout compared to regular ones—like the 2021 recall turnout being around 58.4%. True, the special election allows for mailed ballots, but low turnout still impacts the legitimacy of the results, even with a narrow majority required for recall.**Analyzing replacement elections**

In a replacement election, it's crucial to note that all voters can participate, whether they voted yes or no on the recall. This setup means that those against the recall can still vote for a replacement. As a result, the replacement candidate might be backed by voters who wanted to keep the incumbent, leading to a situation where the replacement doesn’t truly reflect the majority that supported the recall. It ultimately hinges on candidate plurality rather than a clear majority in recall support.**Evaluating electoral measures**

In a normal election, the principle is one person, one vote, leading to a pluralistically elected winner. However, if a winner only serves an unexpired term, their position can be temporary. For instance, in California, a recall replacement can serve a significant portion of the original term, like the 2003 recall. If I say NO to a proposed fix requiring a runoff when no one gets a majority, am I supporting the current plurality system? Saying NO could limit replacement options without further legislative changes.**Considering electoral reforms**

The Little Hoover Commission's proposed "snap special election" offers a majoritarian solution, but it also needs an amendment, and legislators opted for a different route. This reform could be rare due to the century-long law currently in place. Prop 5 has its specific tradeoffs, such as placing the incumbent on the same ballot. If the incumbent loses, the successor must have more votes, but they might still win without a majority. This approach supports direct voter choice while discouraging recalls that replace an official with a less popular alternative.**Assessing Prop 5 options**

Prop 5 removes the second question from elections but doesn't offer an alternative proposal. A potentially better option could be a two-stage election featuring the top two candidates. While Prop 5 includes a special election for the legislature and Governor, I wonder if it creates a plurality for other executive appointments, which aren't directly voted on. Originally, a runoff could have been a possibility. So, the choice comes down to the current system versus Prop 5, which isn't perfect either. The recall process also incurs millions, making claims about reducing expenses appear weak.**Analyzing recall propositions**

This measure isn’t about reducing waste; it's about who gets to be in office. The recall aims to remove officials, not to create special elections that reward the best candidate in a crowded field. The current system mismatches majoritarian ideals since a majority can remove someone, but the replacement is selected by a plurality. This invites partisan misuse and can derail normal elections. Prop 5 keeps the recall option for voters, with reasonable succession rules from established processes.**Evaluating the recall process**

When an official is recalled, they can run again in a subsequent special election, allowing voters to choose in a more traditional format, but maybe that's a bit too lenient. The officeholder is immediately removed, so they're not protected. While appointing statewide officials for midterm vacancies gives the governor authority (with legislative confirmation), it temporarily limits voter choice. Crowded replacement ballots can confuse voters, leading to many blanks. A simple yes/no option may improve clarity. I’m considering the proposition regarding future elections, but it has some significant flaws. For one, not all successor votes create pluralities after special elections. The process varies between state elections, like top-two and runoffs. Another issue is that allowing someone to run again could be problematic — if voters recall someone but they win again in a subsequent election, it means their earlier decision might be reversed. This makes the recall process less straightforward.**Evaluating recall votes**

The recall vote is a straightforward yes or no question, allowing voters to change their minds. In cases of direct democracy, the ability to recall can lead to an election. For governors, if a recall occurs early enough, voters elect a new governor by majority, even if the current one runs again. Regarding Lieutenant Governors, they might serve the remainder of the term following a midterm recall, and the voters' desire for change isn’t always guaranteed; misconduct can be the reason for a recall.**Assessing the recall process**

While a recall might seem more democratic, it can actually complicate voter choice since the direct election of officials is somewhat reduced. In the current system, recall ballots include a replacement vote even if the recall fails, which can confuse voters. This setup diverts attention from the essential question of whether an official should be recalled. Separating these issues could help voters focus better. p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Is a hissy fit worth $200 million (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-02-03/california-recall-election-cost-200-million-dollars)?
That was the tab in 2021, when California held a recall election (https://www.latimes.com/topic/newsom-recall) less than a year before Gov. Gavin Newsom was set to face voters.
There was angst —the COVID-19 pandemic was raging (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-08-19/l-a-county-covid-19-deaths-top-25000-as-delta-spreads). There was anger — the lifesaving restrictions (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-12-13/california-orders-statewide-mask-order-starting-wednesday) imposed by Washington and Sacramento made daily living a chore (https://www.latimes.com/science/coronavirus-one-year-later) and drove many small businesses to the brink. Others went clear over the edge (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2020-10-29/coronavirus-pandemic-small-business-southern-california).
There was also no small amount of political opportunism at play.
The recall gave Newsom’s critics, mainly on the right, a chance to try to chase the Democrat from an office (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-08-27/recall-backers-have-california-ideas-beyond-newsom-defeat) that Republicans, under normal circumstances, stood little chance of winning.
Advertisement
In the end, the recall effort amounted to scarcely more than a partisan tantrum. The result — 61.9% voting no, 38.1% voting yes (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2021-09-14/recall-election-california-newsom-results) — matched the outcome of the 2018 gubernatorial race (https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-california-governor-race-20181106-story.html) down to the decimal. All that money and effort wasted on an election in which voters said pretty much, yep, we meant what we said. Not too long after, they gave Newsom a second term (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2022-11-08/2022-california-election-governor-newsom-dahle-results).
The plebiscite, and its pointlessness (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-09-15/newsom-california-recall-election-costly-lessons), underscored the many flaws inherent in California’s recall system. In November, voters will get a chance to remedy at least one of them, eliminating the chance a candidate could take office with just marginal support from voters.

One choice, not two
Currently, a recall election is conducted in two parts. Voters are asked whether a lawmaker should be removed and, if so, who their replacement should be. If the incumbent is ousted, whoever gets the most votes takes their place, even if they fall well shy of attaining majority support. (Which is not out of the question in a large multi-candidate field; in 2003, 135 people were on the ballot (https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2003-aug-27-me-recallqa27-story.html), vying to replace Gov. Gray Davis (https://www.latimes.com/la-100703recall_lat-story.html).)
Among its provisions, Proposition 5 would amend the state Constitution so that voters would be asked a simple yes-or-no question: Do you wish to recall the incumbent? If so, the lieutenant governor would serve as governor for the rest of the ousted executive’s term — unless the recall occurred during the first two years a governor was in office and before the filing deadline for the next statewide election.
In that case, a special election would be held on the same date as the next primary and a candidate receiving a majority of votes would serve out the governor’s term. If no candidate received a majority, the top-two finishers would face each other in a November runoff, with the winner taking over as governor.
Still there?
Proposition 5 has two benefits. It would save taxpayer dollars by consolidating elections and it would enhance the legitimacy and political standing of a replacement governor by ensuring he or she assumed office with at least 50% support.
But there’s still more to be done (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2022-06-23/california-recall-reform-efforts-stall).
Ending political promiscuity
California makes it way too easy to qualify a gubernatorial recall measure.
Of the 19 states that allow their governor to be booted, California is by far the most permissive. Forcing an election requires signatures reflecting just 12% of the ballots cast in the prior gubernatorial contest. In Newsom’s case, proponents needed just under 1.5 million signatures in a state with more than 22 million voters and nearly 40 million residents.
Not exactly a thundering roar.
The threshold should be higher and the reasons for kicking a governor out of office should be more serious, such as corruption, official malfeasance or conviction for a serious crime. Not just because a governor is a member of the opposite party (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-03-01/newsom-recall-sore-losers-are-undermining-democracy), orpeople on the losing end (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2021-04-13/newsom-recall-revolt-red-vs-blue-california) of an election are unhappy with the result.

**Analyzing Proposition 5**

On September 9, the pro argument acknowledges that there's still more to discuss, particularly regarding the claim about "less than majority" from 2003. A candidate received 48.6% for replacement votes but was only slightly below the majority. In the case of a recall, it’s true that taxpayer dollars could be saved through consolidation. The costs of the initial recall were significant, but subsequent elections could potentially reduce overall spending. The plausibility of Prop 5 saving costs is interesting!**Evaluating Election Costs and Reforms**

The removal election does incur costs. For state legislatures, a separate special election may not be consolidated with the regular schedule, leading to additional expenses. The League of California Cities has mentioned both possibilities. A good reform could indeed be beneficial. Proposition 5 aims to ensure that a successor after a gubernatorial recall is elected through a top-two election or by statewide vote for the Lt. Governor. The Little Hoover Commission recommended a single "snap" election for all candidates, comparing the incumbent to potential successors while giving voters better options.**Exploring Proposition 5's Design**

Proposition 5 closely resembles what many states with frequent recalls do. It's worth considering whether it's better to include the incumbent on the ballot in a single snap election, allowing voters to choose between the incumbent and alternatives. But if, for example, the incumbent wins 40% while others split 60%, they would remain in office, and recalls might not reflect majority sentiment. A solution could be a compulsory runoff if no majority is reached, but that could add costs to the election process.**Analyzing ranked-choice voting**

I'm considering whether voters are familiar with ranked-choice voting (RCV). California currently uses it in some cities, but not statewide, which might complicate recall efforts. I wonder if voters could initiate future propositions for RCV if this proposal fails. There's a principle about rejecting flawed proposals, emphasizing targeted reforms instead. However, that might leave the status quo unchallenged. It seems political momentum from 2021 influences the current proposals, but maybe waiting for a better alternative isn't so bad since bad outcomes are rare.

Proposition 5
Delay replacing recalled state officials
Under current law, after choosing whether to recall an elected official, voters are asked who should replace them. This constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by state lawmakers, would delay the election of a successor until a separate election. The recalled officer would be allowed to run in that election. If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over their duties until a new governor is elected. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.
BEGIN → (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/propositions/quizzes)
Support
Oppose
Summary
Support
Proposition 5 is a constitutional amendment born out of a proposal from the secretary of state’s office following the unsuccessful recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. Secretary of State Shirley Weber told lawmakers her office felt a recall election should focus on whether the elected official should be recalled, not whether other potential candidates would be better in the role. Democrat Josh Newman, who was successfully recalled from his state Senate seat in 2018, authored the measure, saying it would reduce the “political gamesmanship” that elevates candidates who otherwise wouldn’t receive a majority of votes.
Oppose
Opponents including the California Republican Party and Election Integrity Project, which advocates for voter ID requirements and restrictions on mail-in voting, argue that allowing the lieutenant governor to assume the governor’s position if the governor were recalled would dissuade people from participating in a recall election. Almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it, arguing that it would dilute the power of voters while protecting incumbents. The current recall process is how former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was first elected in 2003.

There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).

Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

I'm thinking about how the special successor election works through plurality voting, where a low-supported candidate can get elected by voters. In contrast, under Prop 5, the governor chooses the appointee. I wonder if a gubernatorial appointee would be seen as more legitimate, especially if they come from a majority-elected governor and have legislative confirmation. However, this doesn't mean voters have a direct say in who takes over when recalling an AG. It raises the question of whether legislative selection is more democratic than public plurality voting.**Considering gubernatorial appointments**

I find it interesting to think about whether a replacement for an office, chosen by a one-party supermajority in the legislature, truly represents the voters. This is particularly relevant for a state constitutional office like Attorney General, which is elected statewide. If the governor appoints a new AG, the next election cycle will happen as scheduled. If a recall occurs early, the next election may still fill the vacancy during the regular cycle, as stated in Article V. However, the voter representation can vary depending on the timing of elections.**Examining AG election terms**

I'm exploring the circumstances around the terms of elected Attorneys General (AG) and what happens if there’s a vacancy. AGs serve four-year terms. If there's a vacancy with two years left, the next regular election could occur after those two years. When an officer is recalled, they can be replaced only until the end of their unexpired term, which can extend up to four years. I see the argument that appointment procedures help maintain continuity, similar to filling vacancies after someone's death. This can create a scenario where there's a vacancy for months, which lowers representation. A district's legislative seat is crucial, especially in closely balanced chambers. If the majority recall voters reject an official but don’t get a representative for a while, it can be frustrating, even if it holds officials accountable.**Analyzing recall election outcomes**

I realize that a candidate could indeed be chosen with just a plurality of votes, even if they get more votes than anyone else. Voters who choose "no recall" can also pick a replacement, which can create confusion—like in the 2003 election where Arnold got more total votes but was second in a recall context. A better method might be to let voters pick all candidates post-recall and have a runoff if no one surpasses 50%. ## Big stick
The California recall applies to all statewide elected officials, members of the state legislature and judges of the appellate and supreme courts.
There’s a low bar to get a recall of statewide elected officials on the ballot: signatures from 12% of the number of those who voted in the previous election for the same office.
The provision features simultaneous recall and replacement elections: If the voters choose to remove the incumbent, the candidate who receives a plurality of the votes becomes governor.
...
Compared to the widely used initiative, state recalls are very rare.
Since 1911, only 11 California state officials have faced recall campaigns that gathered enough signatures to make the ballot.
Of those, only six were actually removed from office: Sen.
Marshall Black, a Republican-Progressive, was removed in 1913 on charges of embezzlement.
A year later, Democrat Edwin E. Grant was removed for sponsorship of Red Light Abatement legislation, which was wildly unpopular in his San Francisco district.
Republican assembly members Paul Horcher and Doris Allen were recalled in an effort spearheaded by their own party in 1994 and 1995, respectively, for crossing party lines in the vote for speaker.

As California’s independent oversight agency, the Little Hoover Commission launched a study in 2021-2022 to consider whether the state’s system for recalling state office-holders should be changed, and if so, how.
The Commission concluded that the recall system should be retained, both because it is substantively valuable—voters should be able to fire an elected official mid-term—and because it is overwhelmingly popular with
voters.
Yet substantial changes are needed in 
California’s recall process.
Current recall procedures breed the possibility of an undemocratic outcome, since they allow a replacement candidate to win office while receiving fewer votes than the incumbent.
There is also concern that the recall is subject to potential overuse or abuse.
In its 2022 report, Reforming the Recall, the 
Commission recommends that California make two key changes to its recall system:
◊
Adjust the signature requirement for recalling statewide office-holders from 12 percent of the vote in the last election for the office to 10 percent of registered voters, thereby increasing the number of signatures necessary to initiate a recall election and creating a more stable signature threshold.
◊
Replace the existing two-part recall ballot with a “snap” special election in which the official targeted for recall is placed on the ballot with all replacement candidates.
This would ensure that no official is recalled and replaced by a successor who receives fewer votes.

Recall ballots have two key questions.
**Should the official be recalled?
If so, then who replaces them?** The official is removed on a majority vote in favor of the recall.
If they are recalled, their replacement is decided by the successor candidate with the most votes, even if it does not constitute a majority.
That design is what produced the 2003 outcome in which then-governor Gray Davis was removed from office and Arnold Schwarzenegger was elected, even though Schwarzenegger had less than a majority among the 135 candidates.

California’s recall ballot asks two separate questions of voters: whether the office-holder should be recalled, and if so, who should replace that person?
The problem is that while the officer-holder must obtain more than half of the vote on the first question to stay in office, a candidate on the second question needs only a plurality to win.
If the office-holder is recalled, whoever gets the most votes on the second question takes the office – no matter what share of the vote they receive.
This means that a replacement candidate can succeed to office while receiving far fewer votes than a recalled incumbent.
...
The other big problem is the signature requirement to trigger a recall election.
That figure is based on the number of votes cast in the last election for the office.
This creates a needlessly unstable threshold, since turnout can vary significantly between elections.
In our new report, “Reforming the Recall,” the commission offers two major reforms to address these weaknesses:
First, California should replace the existing two-part recall ballot with a “snap” special election, in which the targeted official appears on the ballot alongside the replacement candidates.

## Ballot Measure Recommendations
### Proposition 5
#### RECALL ELECTION REFORM FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS
California’s recall gives voters a way to remove a corrupt or failed official.
It should never become a back door to state office for a replacement candidate propped up by only a small fraction of voters.
However, that is exactly what today’s recall rules allow, since the same ballot that decides removal also determines a replacement based on whoever gets the most votes, even if that’s far short of a majority.
Prop 5 fixes a built-in contradiction in the recall process.

## LEGISLATIVE COUNSEL'S DIGEST
This measure would eliminate the successor election for a recalled state officer and instead provide, in the event an officer is removed in a recall election, that the office will remain vacant until it is filled in accordance with the Constitution and statute.
The measure would repeal the prohibition against the officer subject to the recall being a candidate to fill the office in a special election, but would prohibit the appointment of the officer subject to the recall election to fill the vacancy.

**Evaluating election replacement preferences**

The 2021 UCSD survey reveals interesting insights: 43% support the idea of the lieutenant governor automatically replacing a governor, while 41% oppose it. There’s also a slight preference for a split replacement election, with 47% in favor. It's compelling that support seems higher among Democrats compared to Republicans, with 61% of Democrats backing replacement only if the recall is successful. The overall picture suggests a nuanced view of voters' preferences that requires further analysis by party affiliation.**Analyzing voter support for proposals**

It seems that the removal of the second question is linked to lower support among voters. In the UCSD survey, there was a 47-37 split, suggesting a potential majority against it, especially when we consider the undecided voters. The governor succession proposal showed weak support at 43-41, while the alternative reform (like a runoff) appears to be more popular. There’s also a chance that allowing candidates to run in special elections could lead to a majority outcome, depending on timing and circumstances. This all seems quite intricate!**Evaluating majoritarian successor benefits**

The main benefit of a majoritarian successor applies primarily to elected governors and legislatures, while the costs related to voter choice affect everyone. This leads me to lean towards a "no" recommendation to preserve direct voter authority. However, I want to remain cautious about final decisions. 

Looking at the measure’s outcome, direct democracy works in two parts: when an elected official loses a recall, the voters' "yes" vote is legitimate, and their right to choose a replacement is important. The candidate with plurality support doesn't always reflect limited backing, as they're often among the available options.**Analyzing electoral systems**

I'm thinking about the complexities of electoral legitimacy, particularly regarding how plurality votes play a role in elections. It seems inconsistent to invoke majority rules for recalls while accepting plurality for initial elections. California uses a Top Two method ensuring majority wins in November, which seems like a viable solution for too many candidates. I also see that for recalls, California allows voters who vote "no" to pick replacements, which might not be ideal, as it can lead to successors with relatively low support.**Examining the recall process**

I'm considering the complexities around recall elections and replacement appointees. For example, a candidate might not win a majority but still have significant voter support. There's also the question of whether a replacement appointee has public backing, which can vary. If a governor is recalled, it seems inconsistent for the Lieutenant Governor, who was elected separately, to automatically take over. Voters may be unhappy with the same political leadership if they sought to remove the governor.**Exploring California's recall process**

California's recall law has been around for over a century and was designed to allow voters to select a successor alongside the recall. This historical context is essential. Under Proposition 5, when a governor is recalled, the appointed nominee is usually confirmed and may share the same political affiliation, which might not significantly change the government. Since recalls are infrequent, voters typically opt to wait for the next election unless there's a pressing ethical concern. This leads me to wonder if the right to immediately replace an official should be a fundamental principle.**Evaluating election processes**

Having a separate election for a successor offers more time to evaluate candidates and follows regular election rules, which often require a majority. The current officeholder might run again, allowing voters to decide if they want that person back. While direct choice is delayed, a replacement will be selected eventually. Interestingly, if voters feel immediate choice is vital, these methods could seem less democratic. Some states have special appointments until the next regular election, which Californians appear to accept during transitions.**Examining recall procedures**

For most elective offices, if a representative resigns or passes away, the successor is either appointed by the Governor or decided through a special election, which seems logically consistent when treating recalls as vacancies. However, with recalls, the officeholder is removed intentionally by a public vote. If the governor or assembly appoints a successor, it makes the public's role in choosing a replacement less direct. Other states handle this with either succession or a separate election. California's combined system is one of the few. Let's look into the historical reasons behind this joint system.**Researching historical context**

I'm diving into the Progressive Era, where corruption was pervasive and often involved whole political machines. The user's request for extensive research makes me think it's important to focus on the exact historical rationale behind these issues. I remember a 2003 historical law article that provides analysis on the topic. It might be helpful to examine both the original constitutional amendment and that article as I prepare to gather more insights.

I'm thinking about the complexities of electoral legitimacy, particularly regarding how plurality votes play a role in elections. It seems inconsistent to invoke majority rules for recalls while accepting plurality for initial elections. California uses a Top Two method ensuring majority wins in November, which seems like a viable solution for too many candidates. I also see that for recalls, California allows voters who vote "no" to pick replacements, which might not be ideal, as it can lead to successors with relatively low support.**Examining the recall process**

I'm considering the complexities around recall elections and replacement appointees. For example, a candidate might not win a majority but still have significant voter support. There's also the question of whether a replacement appointee has public backing, which can vary. If a governor is recalled, it seems inconsistent for the Lieutenant Governor, who was elected separately, to automatically take over. Voters may be unhappy with the same political leadership if they sought to remove the governor.**Exploring California's recall process**

California's recall law has been around for over a century and was designed to allow voters to select a successor alongside the recall. This historical context is essential. Under Proposition 5, when a governor is recalled, the appointed nominee is usually confirmed and may share the same political affiliation, which might not significantly change the government. Since recalls are infrequent, voters typically opt to wait for the next election unless there's a pressing ethical concern. However, with recalls, the officeholder is removed intentionally by a public vote. If the governor or assembly appoints a successor, it makes the public's role in choosing a replacement less direct. 37 | 2013 La démocratie directe à l'épreuve du temps (https://journals.openedition.org/siecles/873)
The People versus the Octopus: California Progressives and the Origins of Direct Democracy
Le peuple contre la Pieuvre : les progressistes californiens et les origines de la démocratie directe
Glen Gendzel
https://doi.org/10.4000/siecles.1109 (https://doi.org/10.4000/siecles.1109)
Abstract | Index | Text | Notes | References | About the author
Abstracts
English Français
Direct democracy, for better or for worse, has become California's most distinctive and emblematic political institution. Initiative, referendum, and recall elections were added to the state constitution in 1911 as part of Governor Hiram Johnson's “progressive” movement, which redeemed the state from control by “The Octopus”, meaning the Southern Pacific Railroad monopoly that had a stranglehold on the state's economy and government. Progressive reformers expected that California voters would use direct democracy to tame the Octopus and to protect themselves against such wealthy special interests in the future. Over time, however, those same interests proved adept at using direct democracy to serve their own interests. This article surveys the origins of direct democracy in California's progressive movement and traces its history up to the 1970s.
La démocratie directe, pour le meilleur ou pour le pire, est devenue l’institution la plus marquante et la plus emblématique de l’État de Californie. Initiative populaire, référendum et révocation des représentants ont été introduits dans la Constitution de l’État en 1911, dans le cadre de la réforme « progressiste » du Gouverneur Hiram Johnson, destinée à soustraire l’État au contrôle de « La Pieuvre », à savoir le monopole de la Compagnie des chemins de fer du Pacifique sud qui avait la mainmise sur l’économie de l’État et le gouvernement. Les réformateurs progressistes pensaient que les électeurs californiens recourraient à la démocratie directe pour « dompter » la Pieuvre et pour se protéger à l’avenir contre des groupes d’intérêt si riches. Avec le temps, cependant, ces derniers se sont avérés très habiles à utiliser la démocratie directe pour servir leurs propres intérêts. Cet article retrace l’histoire de la démocratie directe, depuis ses origines – qu’elle puise dans le mouvement progressiste de Californie – jusqu’aux années 1970.

3 See, for example, “The Ungovernable State,” The Economist 391 (May 16, 2009): 33-36; Joel Stein, “S (...)
1 Direct democracy is an old idea that has come a long way from its origins in ancient Greece. In the United States, direct democracy is a political artifact of the Progressive Era left over from the early twentieth century. Almost every state with direct democracy adopted it at that time; none adopted it before 1898 and very few have since 1920. 1 Direct democracy in the United States is also a regional phenomenon of the American West. About half of the fifty states have direct democracy, but 80% of them are in the West. 2 And of course, no state has made more use of direct democracy, for good or ill, than has California, the big western tail that wags the American dog when it comes to direct democracy and just about everything else. In recent years it has become fashionable among media pundits to blame direct democracy for California’s political paralysis and financial basket-case status. 3 So how did California become America’s poster child for reform gone awry and for good intentions leading to catastrophic unintended consequences ?
4 John Hoyt Williams, A Great and Shining Road: The Epic Story of the Transcontinental Railroad (New (...)
5 Richard J. Orsi, Sunset Limited: The Southern Pacific Railroad and the Development of the American (...)
2 The story of how direct democracy turned California into a political train wreck begins, appropriately enough, with a railroad. Californians had high hopes for the transcontinental railroad project, completed in 1869 with generous public subsidies. The railroad was supposed to usher in a new era of rapid growth and prosperity for California. By connecting the state more closely to the rest of the United States, the railroad could bring people out west, while carrying the products of California’s farms and factories back east. 4 Most Californians imagined that the railroad would be a simple, benign technology, but in fact it was a monopoly corporation, known as the Central Pacific Railroad, which soon enjoyed near-total control over all transportation into, out of, and within the state – and this corporation was anything but benign. Some historians praise the railroad for its contributions to California’s growth and development; it certainly did represent a drastic improvement in transportation efficiency over the days of covered wagons, stagecoaches, and sailing ships. 5
6 White, Railroaded ; Charles Edward Russell, Stories of the Great Railroads (Chicago: Charles H. Kerr (...)
7 Russell, Stories of the Great Railroads, 281-308; Stuart Daggett, Chapters on the History of the So (...)
8 Crocker quoted in Joseph S. O’Flaherty, An End and a Beginning: The South Coast and Los Angeles, 18 (...)
3 No one suggests that the railroad on balance was bad for California, given that the state’s agriculture, industry, and commerce all depended on it. The railroad was California’s biggest employer and biggest private landowner; it promoted local products and lured hordes of tourists and settlers to the state as well. The problem with the railroad was that it insisted on controlling California’s growth and development for its own benefit while reaping an unfair share of the profits. 6 In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, California suffered from some of the highest, most complicated, and least predictable railroad rates in the world. Charges for carrying passengers and freight varied capriciously between different destinations, different customers, and for different cargoes; rates also changed constantly, rising and falling not with actual railroad costs but with the market price of products being transported. The railroad, not the producer, grabbed most of the profit to be earned by shipping products from one place to another. As a result, California’s farmers, merchants, and manufacturers often found themselves priced out of national markets due to transportation costs. 7 And the railroad routinely blackmailed California towns and cities into handing over taxpayer subsidies and land grants in exchange for the privilege of a rail connection. Charles Crocker, co-owner of the Central Pacific, told the Los Angeles City Council in 1872 that if they did not pay the ransom he demanded, “I will make the grass grow in the streets of your city.” 8 Nowadays large employers and professional sports teams play this hardball game of corporate blackmail, but western railroads such as the Central Pacific invented the technique in the late nineteenth century. In 1882, the Central Pacific changed its name to the Southern Pacific after a complex merger, but it was the same railroad company with the same monopoly power – and with increasing political power as well.
9 Debates and Proceedings of the Constitutional Convention of the State of California, Convened at th (...)
10 McAfee, California’s Railroad Era, 91-217; Alexander Callow, Jr., “The Legislature of a Thousand Sc (...)
11 “Bribery in California,” New York Times, Aug. 17, 1891; Salvador A. Ramirez, ed., The Octopus Speak (...)
4 California adopted a new constitution in 1879 to start regulating and taxing the railroad, and this seems to have spurred the company into politics. 9 Railroad lobbyists and attorneys dispensed a torrent of bribes and favors to “influence” California legislators, officials, judges, and newspaper editors in exchange for favorable legislation, regulations, rulings, and press coverage. Behind the scenes, agents of the Southern Pacific controlled party conventions, legislative sessions, court hearings, regulatory decisions, and even the outcomes of elections. 10 Corruption in California politics was like wind or gravity: people couldn’t see it directly, but they could observe its effects in the form of relentlessly pro-railroad public policy, year after year. Periodic upsurges of reform failed to bring the Southern Pacific to heel; the company went on charging high rates, paying low taxes, blackmailing communities, monopolizing land, and paying off politicians while soaking up subsidies and tax breaks. 11 California was not unique in this regard: many western states in the late nineteenth century suffered from the twin evils of corporate domination and political corruption. But California was exceptional in the extent to which it was dominated by a single corporation: the Southern Pacific Railroad, locally known as “The Octopus.”
12 Frank Norris, The Octopus: The Epic of Wheat, A Story of California (New York: Collier, 1901). See (...)
13 R. Hal Williams, The Democratic Party and California Politics, 1880-1896 (Stanford, CA: Stanford Un (...)
14 Samuel G. Blythe, “Putting the Rollers Under the S.P.,” Saturday Evening Post 183 (Jan. 7, 1911): 6 (...)
5 Long before Frank Norris’ novel by that name appeared in 1901, California cartoonists were depicting the railroad as a monster Octopus with tentacles of steel wrapped around farmers, workers, merchants, and manufacturers, squeezing the lifeblood of commerce out of them. 12 After 1900, Californians watched with envy as self-styled “progressives” gained power in other states and brought their corporate adversaries to heel, notably in Wisconsin under Governor Robert La Follette. Why not in California, too? Anti-railroad reformers in California did wage several campaigns through the Populist party and the Democratic party without success in the 1890s and 1900s, but the breakthrough came in 1910, when progressives seized control of the state’s Republican party. 13 They nominated Hiram Johnson, a fiery anti-railroad attorney, to run for governor that year. Johnson had distinguished himself as lead prosecutor in the San Francisco graft trials of 1906 to 1909, when he put San Francisco’s corrupt political boss behind bars. Hence there was reason to believe that when Johnson vowed to “kick the railroad out of politics,” he meant it. Johnson and his fellow progressive Republicans swept the state elections of 1910, and when the next state legislature gathered in 1911, reformers had control at last. 14 They did not, however, presume that their victory would be permanent. Governor Johnson and his comrades expected that the Octopus would recover from its temporary setback and somehow outmaneuver them in the next election. This is why California progressives acted so boldly after their smashing victory in 1910, because they figured they might have only one chance to tame the Octopus.
15 Franklin Hichborn, Story of the Session of the California Legislature of 1911 (San Francisco: James (...)
16 Spencer C. Olin, Jr., California’s Prodigal Sons: Hiram Johnson and the Progressives, 1911-1917 (Be (...)
17 Ida Husted Harper, The History of Woman Suffrage, Vol. 6 (New York: National American Woman Suffrag (...)
6 The 1911 session of the California legislature ranks as the single most important session ever held in the history of the state. Besides passing landmark legislation to regulate the railroad, and other major reforms of state government, the progressives also acted to permanently increase the power of California voters. 15 Governor Johnson and his fellow progressives believed that more democracy was the best way to prevent a return of political corruption and corporate rule in the future. Confident in the people’s wisdom, the progressives assumed that more power in the people’s hands would mean less power for the Southern Pacific or any other wealthy interest that might try to dominate state government in the future. 16 As a sign of their trust in voters, the progressives quickly approved woman suffrage, and California would become the sixth state in the nation, by far the largest yet, to let women vote. 17 But woman suffrage, which practically doubled the size of the electorate overnight, was not the only technique that the progressives had in mind for increasing democracy. As Governor Johnson said in his 1911 inaugural address:
18 Inaugural Address of Governor Hiram W. Johnson Before the Senate and Assembly of the State of Calif (...)
“How best can we arm the people to protect themselves hereafter? . . . We can give to the people the means by which they may accomplish such other reforms as they desire, [and] the means as well by which they may prevent the misuse of the power. . . .The first step in our design to preserve and perpetuate popular government shall be the adoption of the initiative, the referendum, and the recall.” 18
19 Goebel, A Government by the People, 25-90; James D. Barnett, The Operation of the Initiative, Refer (...)
20 V. O. Key, Jr., and Winston W. Crouch, The Initiative and the Referendum in California (Berkeley: U (...)
7 By 1911, California progressives were already familiar with these basic mechanisms of direct democracy. Progressive reformers across the American West were taking up the initiative, the referendum, and the recall as promising solutions to problems of corruption and corporate influence in politics. Starting with South Dakota in 1898, eight western states had recently adopted direct democracy, including California’s neighboring state of Oregon in 1902. Progressives in Oregon used direct democracy to enact sweeping electoral reforms, and there was hope that California might follow suit – especially since several California cities and towns had already adopted direct democracy on the local level and had even begun using it. 19 California’s leading advocate for direct democracy was Dr. John Randolph Haynes, a wealthy physician and real estate investor in Los Angeles who developed a strong interest in this particular reform. Dr. Haynes founded the Direct Legislation League in 1900 and for decades he devoted his time and his sizeable fortune to lobbying and publicity on behalf of direct democracy. 20 Haynes helped convince many progressives, including Governor Johnson, that direct democracy was the best insurance policy against future corruption. As Haynes explained:
21 John R. Haynes speech to the University Club, 1909, as quoted in Laura Tallian, Direct Democracy: A (...)
“Even the election of good men to office . . . frequently fails to produce any marked effect because these men often . . . fail to preserve their integrity. . . . The remedy is a plain and simple one. . . . Give the honest majority . . . the power to initiate and enact legislation which their legislative bodies . . . may refuse; this is the initiative. Give to the honest majority the power to veto the undesired acts of their legislature; this is the referendum. Give to the same honest majority the power to discharge from office at any time the inefficient and incompetent . . . public servant; this is the recall.” 21
22 Hichborn, Story of the Session of the California Legislature of 1911, 20, 93-101, 137-142; Key and (...)
23 Samuel E. Moffett, “Constitutional Referendum in California,” Political Science Quarterly 13 (Mar. (...)
24 Inaugural Address of Governor Johnson, 5.
8 Although he never ran for office himself, Dr. Haynes was a savvy politician. He remained non-partisan while soliciting endorsements from labor and reform groups and extracting pledges of support from candidates in both parties. Governor Johnson let Dr. Haynes help draft the direct democracy amendments to the state constitution, which the legislature approved in 1911. 22 Californians were already accustomed to voting on constitutional amendments passed by the legislature; but the initiative, the referendum, and the recall would give them the power to legislate directly for

CALIFORNIA’S RECALL IS NOT OVERPOWERED
David A. Carrillo, Joshua Spivak, Natalie Kaliss & Jared
Madnick*
The recall is one of three direct democracy tools in California.
Following the failed 2021 recall attempt against California Governor
Gavin Newsom, the state recall process has been criticized for evolving
beyond its intended purpose to the point of being overpowered and prone
to abuse. After reviewing the recall’s original intent, we conduct a
quantitative analysis of state and local recall attempts in California and
compare this to other recall states. We conclude that the critique is
unjustified. In California and elsewhere, state official recalls are
frequently attempted but rarely qualify for the ballot, demonstrating that
the existing recall system is an effective filter. We validate the charge
that the recall is primarily a tool of out-party interests, but conclude that
this is an intended design feature rather than an unanticipated defect.
We conclude instead that California’s local recall is the better target for
reform efforts, given its comparatively easier qualifying requirements,
greater use, and higher success rates. Rather than deviating from its
intended purpose, in its 110 years the California state official recall
proved to be exactly what its Progressive designers intended: a voter
weapon to menace and remove public officials, but one that is difficult
to deploy. We frame the recall as less about politics and more about
policy: recalls function as public opinion or policy polls and overall tend
to validate existing policy. Finally, we conclude that most proposed
reforms are solutions seeking a problem, and that California’s recall
system merits just a few small procedural changes. The upshot is that
the view of California’s recall as a force gone amok is incorrect.
* David A. Carrillo is a Lecturer in Residence and the Executive Director of the
California Constitution Center at the University of California, Berkeley School of Law.
Joshua Spivak is a Senior Fellow at the Hugh L. Carey Institute for Government Reform at
Wagner College and a Senior Research Fellow at the California Constitution Center. Natalie
Kaliss and Jared Madnick are research fellows at the California Constitution Center.

I. INTRODUCTION
The recall is a century-old direct democracy tool for voting out an
elected official before their term ends. This article addresses three
issues: how California’s state and local recall processes perform,
whether the California recall process is overpowered, and the merits of
certain proposed reforms to the state recall. To evaluate claims that
California’s recall is overpowered, we analyze all California state-level
recalls and a sample of local-level recalls and compare those California
data with data from other recall states. From that quantitative analysis
we conclude that in California the recall has been employed often and
with significant success at the local level, and less frequently and with
less success at the state level. Given those results and the experience of
other states with various proposed reforms, we conclude that most
proposed changes to California’s state-level recall are at best
unwarranted, and at worst, will neuter the recall.
At the state level in California the recall is frequently attempted but
rarely successful. From 1911 to 2021, California voters filed 179 recall
petitions against state officials; only 11 qualified (6% of filed) and 6
succeeded (54.5% of qualified), resulting in 5 recalled legislators and 1
recalled governor.1 The other 173 petitions either failed to qualify or
were rejected at the ballot, an overall 96.6% failure rate.2 This shows
that recalls rarely qualify or result in a vacated office, which rebuts
claims that the recall is overused.
At the local level the recall is attempted even more than at the state
level and with greater success.3 We analyzed all California local recalls
from 2011 to 2021 and found that in 555 completed recall drives, 139
petitions qualified (25% of filed) and 86 (61.9% of qualified) succeeded
at the ballot.4 The 469 petitions that either failed to qualify or lost at the
ballot constitute an overall 84.5% percent failure rate. Other states
mirror this result, where the vast majority of recall attempts never reach
the ballot.
Our review of a decade of local California recalls shows that far
more recall petitions are filed at the local versus the state level, that local

II. RECALL DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS
A. The recall in general
A recall is a procedure for removing and replacing a public official
by plebiscite before that official’s term ends.5 It is a political process in
which proponents file a petition, gather signatures, campaign for their
position, and seek a win at the ballot.6 Nineteen states and the District
of Columbia permit recalling at least some state officials.7 At least 41
states and the District of Columbia permit local recall elections.8 Recall
states all share several basic elements:

The recall makes representative government more responsive to
majority will.9 This is consistent with California’s expressly voter-

Hiram Johnson asked, “How best can we arm the people to protect
themselves hereafter?”11 The ballot argument framed the recall as the
power “to remove a dishonest, incapable, or unsatisfactory servant.”12 It
also described the recall as a means to require a public servant “whose
stewardship is questioned . . . to submit the question of his continuance
in office to a vote of the electors. If a majority of all voting at the election
say that their servant is unfit to serve them longer, he is thereby
retired.”13 From their inception in California the recall and other direct
democracy powers commanded strong public support and were adopted
by large majorities.14 Periodic calls to abandon or weaken the recall are
commonly met with “strong popular disapproval.”15 Modern polling

B. Designing a recall system
We frame recall systems as choices between availability and
integrity.17 A recall should be easy enough to deploy that it is both a
credible threat to a targeted official and a realistic means for the voters
to remove that official.18 Yet ballot integrity must be protected so that
the process is not abused. There is a subjective element here. Elected
officials, for example, are likely to view the recall as too easy to use,
given their self-interested view that the electorate should not be
empowered to vote out officials. Voters are likely to be unhappy with
how costly and time-consuming it is to gather enough signatures to
qualify a recall for the ballot, given their self-interested view that it
should be easier to achieve their political aims. And there is a normative
question here about what constitutes a bad elected official.
The answer to these subjective and normative questions is that (like
other direct democracy tools) the recall is a mechanism to enforce
majority will, with the underlying assumption that the majority’s will is
the conclusive answer. Thus, the electorate’s decision to retain or recall
an elected official is itself the answer to the normative question: recalling
an official proves that a majority viewed them as a bad public servant.
Accordingly, the question about whether it should be more or less
difficult to secure that voter opinion turns less on how easy or hard the
recall should be to use, and more on practical effects of a recall system’s
design: whether that design makes the system prone to abuse, or if the
design makes the recall impractical to use at all.

The Progressives intended that the new direct democracy tools
would “give to the electorate the power of action when desired, and . . .

The Progressives intended that direct democracy would ensure that
political power remained in the electorate’s hands, allowing them to
make policy, rescind government actions, or remove corrupt officials
from power between elections.26 Thus, the recall’s intended purpose is
for voters to hold elected officials accountable.27 California voters
overwhelmingly (76%) adopted the recall in October 1911.28
